title: Teacher- Versus AI-Generated (Poe Application) Corrective Feedback and Language Learners’ Writing Anxiety, Complexity, Fluency, and Accuracy
venue: International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-generated written corrective feedback, delivered through the Poe application, is as effective as or more effective than traditional teacher-generated feedback for improving second-language writing. The study focuses on four outcomes: writing anxiety, writing complexity, writing fluency, and writing accuracy. The central question is whether AI-based feedback can reduce learners’ anxiety and improve their writing performance relative to teacher feedback and a no-feedback condition.

The intervention compared three intact classes: one class received teacher corrective feedback, one class received AI-generated corrective feedback via Poe, and one class received no corrective feedback. Students in the AI group were trained to submit their writing to Poe and request revisions, edits, and paraphrasing with attention to grammar, coherence, accuracy, and complexity. The study used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design and analyzed outcomes using one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc comparisons. Writing measures included syntactic complexity indices, fluency measures such as total words and T-units, and accuracy indicators such as error-free clauses and T-units; writing anxiety was measured with a scale developed for the study.

Participants were 75 undergraduate EFL learners enrolled in online writing courses at the School of Foreign Studies, East China University of Political Science and Law in China. All participants were native Mandarin speakers learning English as a second language. The intervention lasted 14 sessions across a semester, and three writing assignments per participant were analyzed across the beginning, middle, and end of the term.

The study concludes that both teacher and AI corrective feedback improved student outcomes compared with no feedback, but AI-generated feedback via Poe generally produced the strongest results. Students in the AI condition showed lower writing anxiety and better performance on reported measures of fluency, accuracy, and complexity than those receiving teacher feedback or no correction. The author argues that AI feedback may offer timely, consistent, and supportive assistance for second-language writing, while also noting limitations related to the small, single-institution sample, lack of long-term follow-up, and uncertain generalizability beyond this specific context and AI tool.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with a comparison group structure, but it is not K-12, uses intact classes, has a small sample, and reports several inconsistencies in outcome labeling and sample counts across tables. It therefore fits a QED with meaningful but notable credibility concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are consistently positive and often large by the paper’s own eta-squared estimates, especially for writing anxiety and several writing-performance measures. However, impact for the target K-12 literacy question should be interpreted cautiously because the sample is undergraduate EFL learners rather than school-age students.

interventions.use_case: Poe application used as an AI-generated corrective feedback tool for EFL student writing, providing revisions, edits, and paraphrasing focused on grammar, accuracy, coherence, and complexity.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental comparison of three intact university EFL classes (AI feedback vs teacher feedback vs no correction; total n=75, 25 per group), AI-generated corrective feedback via Poe outperformed teacher feedback and no-feedback on multiple writing outcomes. Reported posttest differences favored AI on accuracy-related measures (EFC/C M=0.80 vs 0.60 vs 0.40; EFT/T M=0.84 vs 0.64 vs 0.40; E/W M=0.85 vs 0.62 vs 0.41), complexity (CT M=2.5 vs 2.0 vs 1.6; DCT M=1.2 vs 0.8 vs 0.6), and fluency/productivity (T-units M=31 vs 28 vs 24; total words M=750 vs 640 vs 590; W/T M=19.5 vs 17.3 vs 15.1), with omnibus ANOVAs reported as significant at p=.001 and eta-squared values ranging roughly from 0.51 to 0.62 for most writing measures.
finding.measure: Writing quality indicators: error-free clauses, error-free T-units, errors per word, clauses per T-unit, dependent clauses per T-unit, total T-units, total words, words per T-unit
finding.effect_size: η² range reported approximately 0.51-0.62 for most writing outcomes; some tables/reporting are inconsistent

finding.finding_summary: The AI-generated feedback group reported the lowest writing anxiety after the intervention compared with teacher feedback and no correction (M=1.60 vs 2.10 vs 2.70; n=25 per group). The omnibus ANOVA was significant (F=53.54, p=.001) with a very large reported effect size (η²=0.70), and Bonferroni comparisons indicated the AI group showed greater anxiety reduction than both comparison groups.
finding.measure: Writing anxiety scale developed for the study
